source_text:
Fragmenta in epistulam ad Galatas (in catenis)
Gal: Prolog
Τοῦ κηρύγματος εἰς τὰ ἔθνη δεχθέντος τινὲς τῶν ἀπὸ τῆς περιτομῆς ἐξιόντες
ἔπειθον τὰ ἔθνη ἰουδαΐζειν, καὶ πρώτη περὶ τούτου φαίνεται ζήτησις γεγενημένη ἐν
Ἀντιοχείᾳ, ὅτι οἱ ἀπόστολοι ἔγραψαν μὴ ὑποκεῖσθαι νόμῳ, ἀπέχεσθαι δὲ
εἰδωλοθύτου καὶ αἵματος καὶ πνικτοῦ καὶ πορνείας· οὕτω γὰρ ἔδοξε τῷ ἁγίῳ
πνεύματι. ἐκράτησε δὲ τὸ νόσημα τοῦτο τῶν Galατῶν συμφώνως ἰουδαΐζειν
βουληθέντων. ἐπείσθησαν δὲ ὑπὸ τῶν διαστρεφόντων λεγόντων, ὡς οἱ λοιποὶ
ἀπόστολοι οὐ κωλύουσι τοὺς βουλομένους τηρεῖν τὸν νόμον. 299 Gal 1,4 ∆είκνυσιν
ὅτι οὐ Μωϋσῆς ἀπέθανεν ὑπὲρ τοῦ κόσμου οὐδέ τις τῶν προφητῶν ἄλλος. οὐ δεῖ
τοίνυν ἡττᾶσθαι τοῦ μὴ σώσαντος, ἀλλὰ τοῦ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἀποθανόντος. Gal 1,6–7 Εἰς
ἕτερον εὐαγγέλιον ὃ οὐκ ἔστιν ἕτερον, φησίν· τὸ γὰρ ἡμέτερον εὐαγγέλιον καὶ τὸ
τῶν ἀποστόλων ἐκτὸς ὑμᾶς εἶναι βούλεται νόμου. Gal 1,8–10 Ἔστω ἄγγελος, διὰ τί
δὲ καὶ ἡ μεῖς; ὅτε ἐκηρύττομεν, πνεύματος ἁγίου δυνάμει ἐκηρύξαμεν· τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα
τὸ ἅγιον οὐ μετανοεῖ. ἐὰν οὖν ἄλλα εἴπωμεν, κατελίπομεν τὰ τοῦ πνεύματος. ἔστω
οὖν καὶ ὁ κῆρυξ ἀνάθεμα, ἀθετῶν τὸ κήρυγμα. Παρ' ὃ παρελάβετε. οὐκ ἐκήρυξα μὲν
ἐγώ, φησίν, ὑμεῖς δὲ οὐκ ἐλάβετε, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐγὼ ἐκήρυξα, καὶ ὑμεῖς παρελάβετε. οὔτε
ἐγὼ μετανοῶ κηρύξας, καὶ ὑμεῖς τηρήσατε ὃ εἰλήφατε. Ἄρτι γὰρ ἀνθρώπους πείθω ἢ
τὸν θεόν; ἢ ζητῶ ἀνθρώποις ἀρέσκειν; εἰ ἔτι ἀνθρώποις ἤρεσκον, Χριστοῦ δοῦλος
οὐκ ἂν ἤμην. μέλλων αὐτοὺς ὑπομιμνήσκειν τοῦ ἰδίου εὐαγγελίου, προλαβὼν
ἀσφαλίζεται ἵνα μὴ νομίσωσιν ὅτι θεραπεύει ὑπαγόμενος· ἐπιπλήττει γὰρ νουθετῶν.
εἰπὼν δὲ εἰ ἔτι, ἐδήλωσεν ὅτι ἤρεσκε ποτὲ ἀνθρώποις. τίσι δὲ ἤρεσκεν; παρ' ὧν
ἔλαβεν ἐπιστολὰς τοὺς εἰς ∆αμασκὸν πιστοὺς κακῶσαι. εἰ οὖν, φησίν, ἤρεσκον ἔτι
τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις, οὐκ ἂν ἐπίστευσα τῷ Χριστῷ. Gal 1,13 Τίς χρεία τῆς ἐν τῷ Ἰουδαϊσμῷ
ἀναστροφῆς ἀλλ' ἵνα δείξῃ, ὅτι οὐ προλήψει δουλεύει ἀλλ' ἀληθείᾳ· οὐ γὰρ μισήσας
τὸν νόμον ὑπέδραμε τὴν χάριν–ἐξεδίκει γὰρ αὐτόν–ἀλλ' εὑρὼν τὸ τέλειον ἀπέστη
τοῦ νόμου. Νῦν δείκνυσιν ὅτι πλέον τι τῶν περὶ Πέτρον ἔχει· οὐ γὰρ ἐζήλωσαν
ἐκεῖνοι ὑπὲρ τοῦ Ἰουδαϊσμοῦ ἀπειθοῦντες τῷ Χριστιανισμῷ ὡς ἐγώ. 300 μὴ τοίνυν
οἰηθῇτε ὅτι μισήσας τὸν νόμον ἦλθον εἰς τὴν χάριν– ἐξεδίκουν γὰρ τὸν νόμον–ἀλλ'
εὗρον τὸ τέλειον, καὶ οὐκ ἐξισῶ τὸν νόμον τῇ τελείᾳ χάριτι. Gal 1,16 Οὐ διαβάλλων
δὲ τοὺς ἀποστόλους τοῦτό φησιν, ἀλλ' ὅτι οὐκ ἐστοίχησα θνητῇ σαρκί. Gal 2,16 Εἰ
γὰρ ἐξ ἔργων οὐδεὶς δικαιοῦται τῶν πόνον φερόντων, ἐκ δὲ πίστεως ὅπου τὸ τῆς
εὐκολίας καὶ τὸ τῆς δικαιοσύνης μέγα, πῶς οὐκ ἀναγκαῖόν φησιν ἐάσαντας νόμον
ἀρκεῖσθαι τῇ χάριτι; ἐξ ἔργων νόμου λέγει μὴ δικαιοῦσθαι, οὐκ ἐξ ἐντολῶν· ἡ γὰρ
ἐντολὴ δικαιοῖ ἀκουομένη, τὸ δὲ ἔργον ἦν τὸ δυσκατόρθωτον. Gal 2,18 Πρὸς τὸν
Πέτρον ὁ λόγος· σὺ κατέλυσας αὐτὰ δόγματι ὅπερ ἀπεστάλη παρ' ὑμῶν τοῖς
pass_a_gloss:
[Edition heading: Fragments on the letter to the Galatians (in the catenas). Galatians: prologue.]
Prologue. When the preaching to the nations had been received, some of those from the circumcision, going out, were persuading the nations to judaize. And the first inquiry about this appears to have happened in Antioch, with the result that the apostles wrote that they are not to be subject to the law, but are to abstain from what is sacrificed to idols and from blood and from what is strangled and from fornication; for so it seemed good to the Holy Spirit. And this sickness took hold of the Galatians, who with one accord wanted to judaize. And they were persuaded by those who were perverting them, who said that the rest of the apostles do not hinder those who want to keep the law.
Galatians 1:4. He shows that it was not Moses who died for the world, nor any other one of the prophets. One must not, then, be worsted by (submit to) the one who did not save, but by the one who died for us.
Galatians 1:6-7. "Into a different gospel, which is not another," he says. For our gospel and the gospel of the apostles wants you to be outside the law.
Galatians 1:8-10. Let it be an angel; but why also we? When we were preaching, we preached by the power of the Holy Spirit; and the Holy Spirit does not repent. If then we say other things, we have left behind the things of the Spirit. Let, then, the preacher also be anathema, if he sets aside the preaching. "Contrary to what you received." It is not that I preached, he says, and you did not receive; rather I preached and you received. Neither do I repent of having preached; and you, keep what you have received. "For now am I persuading men, or God? Or am I seeking to please men? If I were still pleasing men, I would not be Christ's slave." Being about to remind them of his own gospel, he secures himself beforehand, so that they may not think that he is flattering them while drawing them on; for he strikes at them while admonishing. Having said "if still," he made plain that he once pleased men. Whom did he please? Those from whom he took letters to harm the believers in Damascus. If then, he says, I were still pleasing the Jews, I would not have believed in Christ.
Galatians 1:13. What need of the conduct in Judaism, except so that he may show that he is a slave not to prejudice but to truth? For it was not from hating the law that he ran in under grace, for he was avenging (defending) the law, but having found the perfect he stood away from the law. Now he shows that he has something more than those around Peter; for those men were not zealous for Judaism, disobeying Christianity, as I was. Do not then suppose that I came to grace from hating the law, for I was defending the law; but I found the perfect, and I do not make the law equal to perfect grace.
Galatians 1:16. Not slandering the apostles does he say this, but that I did not keep in step with mortal flesh.
Galatians 2:16. For if no one is justified from works, the ones that bring toil, but from faith, where the ease is great and the righteousness is great, how is it not necessary, he says, that having let the law go we be content with grace? He says one is not justified from works of the law, not from commandments; for the commandment justifies when it is heard (obeyed), but the work was the thing hard to carry out.
Galatians 2:18. The word is to Peter: You abolished them by a decree, which was sent from you to the [continues in the next section]
pass_b_english: Preface to Galatians: After the Gentiles had accepted the preaching, some of the circumcised went out and tried to persuade the Gentiles to live like Jews. The first inquiry into this seems to have been held at Antioch, and the result was that the apostles wrote that the Gentiles were not to be bound by the law. They were only to keep away from food offered to idols, from blood, from what is strangled and from fornication, “for so it seemed good to the Holy Spirit” (Acts 15:28–29). This sickness took hold of the Galatians, and they agreed together that they wanted to live like Jews. They had been talked into it by men who were leading them astray and claiming that the other apostles put no obstacle in the way of anyone who wanted to keep the law.
On Galatians 1:4: He shows that it was not Moses who died for the world, and not any other prophet either. So we must not give way to the one who did not save us, but to the one who died for us.
On Galatians 1:6–7: “To a different gospel, which is not another,” he says. For our gospel and the gospel of the apostles both want you free of the law.

On Galatians 1:8–10: An angel, granted; but why include “we”? When we preached, we preached in the power of the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit does not change his mind. So if we say something else, we have abandoned what belongs to the Spirit. Then let the preacher too be anathema, if he sets the preaching aside. “Contrary to what you received”: it is not, he says, that I preached and you failed to receive. I preached, and you received. I do not regret my preaching; so you must keep what you were given. “For am I now persuading men, or God? Or am I trying to please men? If I were still pleasing men, I would not be a slave of Christ.” He is about to remind them of his own gospel, so he guards himself in advance. He does not want them to think he is flattering them to win them over, because he is in fact striking at them as he warns them. By saying “if still,” he made it clear that he did once please men. Which men? The ones who gave him letters to harm the believers in Damascus (Acts 9:1–2). So, he says, if I were still pleasing the Jews, I would not have believed in Christ.

On Galatians 1:13: Why speak of his former life in Judaism at all? To show that he serves the truth, not a prejudice. He did not hate the law and so take shelter under grace; he was the law’s champion. He found what is perfect, and that is why he left the law. Now he shows that he has something beyond Peter and those with him: they were never zealots for Judaism who fought against the Christian faith, as I was. So do not imagine that I came to grace out of hatred for the law. I was the law’s defender. But I found what is perfect, and I will not rank the law with grace, which is perfect.
On Galatians 1:16: He does not say this to disparage the apostles. He means that he did not fall in line with mortal flesh.

On Galatians 2:16: No one is justified by works, which bring hard labour, but by faith, where both the ease and the righteousness are great. If so, he says, how can we avoid letting the law go and being content with grace? He says no one is justified by works of the law; he does not say “by commandments.” A commandment justifies when it is heeded; it was the work that was so hard to carry out.

lemmas.gloss: to live like a Jew, keep Jewish customs (Galatians 2:14)
inquiry, debate (the Antioch dispute of Acts 15)
be worsted by, give way to (+ genitive)
court, flatter; draw on, win over
run under (for shelter), take refuge in
make equal, put on a level
keep in line with, fall in step with

choices.why: Edition label for the introductory note; rendered once as a plain lead-in. The work-title line of the edition is not printed in the reading text.
rejected: Regarding the proclamation (old English, which dropped the label and garbled the clause)

choices.term: Ἔστω ἄγγελος, διὰ τί δὲ καὶ ἡμεῖς;
choices.english: An angel, granted; but why include “we”?
choices.why: Severian asks why Paul puts himself ('we') under the anathema of 1:8 alongside an angel; the old English 'Let him be an angel, why then also we?' was unreadable.
rejected: Let him be an angel, why then also we?

choices.english: flattering them to win them over
choices.why: θεραπεύω here is 'court, pay court to' (the issue of 1:10, pleasing men), not 'heal'.
Echo of 'flesh and blood' (1:16); θνητός is 'mortal'.

choices.english: A commandment justifies when it is heeded
choices.why: ἀκούω in the passive of a command = be listened to, obeyed.

choices.term: μὴ τοίνυν οἰηθῇτε … τῇ τελείᾳ χάριτι
choices.why: Restates the preceding third-person sentence in Paul's own voice, with an added clause ('I will not rank the law with grace'); it is the same note continuing, not a second catena form, so it is kept.

choices.english: Peter and those with him … as I was
choices.why: οἱ περὶ Πέτρον = Peter's circle; the switch to 'I' is in the Greek (Paul's voice) and is kept.
The Greek sentence runs on into u01-rem-early ('Ἀντιοχεῦσι'); the English ends with an ellipsis, no text moved.
